design_detail: Repeated cross-sectional comparison of two independent NIAAA national face-to-face surveys of US adults aged 18 or older in households and selected group quarters: NESARC Wave 1 (April 2001 to June 2002; n = 43,093; AUDADIS-IV) and NESARC-III (April 2012 to June 2013; n = 36,309; AUDADIS-5). Weighted 12-month prevalence of any alcohol use, high-risk drinking (exceeding 4 US standard drinks of 14 g in a day for women or 5 for men at least weekly), DSM-IV alcohol use disorder (AUD), and DSM-IV AUD among people who drank and among people who drank at high risk, overall and in 28 sociodemographic subgroups; differences between surveys tested with two-sided t tests on design-based standard errors (SUDAAN). Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as this round's brief directs for national prevalence surveys.
can_establish: Whether two NIAAA national surveys conducted 11 years apart with closely similar questions produced different weighted prevalences of self-reported past-year drinking, weekly high-risk drinking and interview-diagnosed DSM-IV AUD, overall and within sociodemographic groups.
cannot_establish: Whether the differences reflect change in the population rather than differences between the surveys (sampling design, review boards and fieldwork, response rates of 81.0% and about 60%, a $90 incentive reported only for NESARC-III (the paper is silent on any NESARC incentive), census weighting base and instrument version), none of which is modelled; why drinking changed; whether change differed between subgroups (no interaction tests); change within people (different people were sampled); or anything about homeless or incarcerated people, whom neither survey covers.

sample.recruitment: NESARC-III: multistage probability sample (counties or groups of contiguous counties, then groups of census blocks, then households, then adults), oversampling black, Asian or Pacific Islander and Hispanic adults; weighted to the 2012 American Community Survey; respondents received $90; protocol approved by the NIH Combined Neuroscience Institutional Review Board and the Westat Institutional Review Board. NESARC 2001-2002: multistage probability sample with counties or county equivalents as primary units, oversampling black and Hispanic adults and young adults; weighted to the 2000 Decennial Census; protocol reviewed and approved by the US Census Bureau and the US Office of Management and Budget (Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: US adults aged 18 or older living in households and selected group quarters. Neither survey covers homeless or incarcerated people, which the authors say may lead to underestimation (Limitations and Strengths, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Sample composition is not tabulated in this paper; Tables 1 to 5 give prevalence for 28 subgroups by sex, race or ethnicity (white, black, Native American, Asian or Pacific Islander, Hispanic), age (18-29, 30-44, 45-64, 65 or older), marital status, education, family income, poverty threshold, urbanicity and region.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (two independent cross-sectional samples). Overall response 81.0% in NESARC (sampling frame 98.5%, household 88.5%, person 93.0%) and, for NESARC-III, 60.0% in the Methods and 60.1% in the Limitations (household 72.0%, person 84.0%).
sample.selection_effects: The overall response rate fell from 81.0% to about 60% between the surveys. Both are weighted for non-response on measured characteristics only, so a change in who agreed to take part could create or hide a change in prevalence. The authors list the lower NESARC-III response rate as a limitation and say weighting facilitated comparison; the other design differences described in the Methods (sampling stages, oversampled groups, approving bodies, incentive, census base, instrument version) are not discussed as possible sources of the change.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in lay-administered interviews: AUDADIS-IV in NESARC and AUDADIS-5 in NESARC-III. Any 12-month alcohol use was asked with identical questions. DSM-IV AUD symptom items are described as virtually identical, with 3 items slightly reworded and 3 abuse questions added in NESARC-III; DSM-IV AUD with and without the added questions was 8.5% vs 8.2% in NESARC (kappa 0.97) and 12.7% vs 12.2% in NESARC-III (kappa 0.98). No biological testing (Methods › Assessments, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Limitations and Strengths, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: US standard drink = 14 g of pure alcohol. High-risk drinking: 4 or more drinks on any day for women and 5 or more for men, said to follow the US dietary guidelines, exceeded at least weekly in the past 12 months. Alcohol use: any drinking in the past 12 months. Volume, beverage type and other patterns are not analysed (Methods › Assessments, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: The same population subgroup in the 2001-2002 survey.
comparison.matching: None. Crude weighted prevalences for each survey, with no adjustment for changes in population composition or for differences in survey design.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The unmeasured factors that matter are the differences between the surveys (fieldwork and interviewers, sampling design, response, incentive, weighting base, instrument version), none of which is modelled or tested beyond the added abuse questions.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV (2001-2002) and AUDADIS-5 (2012-2013). DSM-IV AUD: dependence (3 or more of 7 criteria) or abuse (1 or more of 4 criteria) in the past 12 months (Methods › Assessments, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability and validity of alcohol use, high-risk drinking and DSM-IV AUD are described as fair to excellent, citing the group's own studies, with no figures in this paper. A NESARC-III validation substudy is said to show similar prevalence and good concordance between AUDADIS and clinician diagnoses of 12-month AUD, also without figures (Methods › Assessments, 4th paragraph; Limitations and Strengths, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Change is reported as the relative percentage change between surveys (the 2012-2013 minus the 2001-2002 prevalence, divided by the 2001-2002 prevalence); absolute differences in percentage points are not reported. Significance refers to the difference between the two weighted prevalences.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five outcomes in the total population and 28 subgroups give 145 between-survey comparisons at P < .05 (editors' count); no test of whether change differed between subgroups.

analysis.effect_sizes: Weighted 12-month prevalence, % (95% CI), 2001-2002 vs 2012-2013, with the printed relative change and the absolute change in percentage points (editors' calculation): alcohol use 65.4 (64.3-66.6) vs 72.7 (71.4-73.9), +11.2%, +7.3 points; high-risk drinking 9.7 (9.3-10.2) vs 12.6 (12.0-13.2), +29.9%, +2.9 points; DSM-IV AUD 8.5 (8.0-8.9) vs 12.7 (12.1-13.3), +49.4%, +4.2 points; AUD among people who drank in the past year 12.9 (interval printed as 12.3-17.5) vs 17.5 (16.7-18.3), +35.7%; AUD among people who drank at high risk 46.5 (44.3-48.7) vs 54.5 (52.7-56.4), +17.2%. DSM-IV AUD by subgroup: men 12.4 vs 16.7 (+34.7%, +4.3 points); women 4.9 vs 9.0 (+83.7%, +4.1); ages 18-29 16.2 vs 23.4 (+44.4%, +7.2); 65 or older 1.5 vs 3.1 (+106.7%, +1.6); white 8.9 vs 13.1 (+47.2%, +4.2); black 6.9 vs 13.3 (+92.8%, +6.4); Hispanic 7.9 vs 12.0 (+51.9%, +4.1); Asian or Pacific Islander 4.5 vs 8.0 (+77.8%, +3.5); Native American 12.1 vs 16.6 and rural 8.8 vs 10.2 (both not significant); family income below $20,000 8.8 vs 14.6 (+65.9%, +5.8). High-risk drinking: women 5.7 vs 9.0 (+57.9%, +3.3 points), men 14.2 vs 16.4 (+15.5%, +2.2), 65 or older 2.3 vs 3.8 (+65.2%, +1.5), black 9.3 vs 15.1 (+62.4%, +5.8). The authors convert these to about 20.2 and 29.6 million adults with high-risk drinking and 17.6 and 29.9 million with DSM-IV AUD.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of two existing surveys; no protocol or analysis plan is referenced.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only relative changes are given; absolute differences and their intervals are not. The Discussion cites other surveys' increases in drinking as corroboration (NHIS +6.0% and NSDUH +9.1% for past-year alcohol use; NHIS +17.8% for 5 or more drinks at least once a year; per capita consumption from sales +6.4%) but not the NSDUH trend in AUD, which the same authors had reported as stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013 (Grant et al., 2015, Discussion, 1st paragraph). The NESARC-III validation substudy is cited without figures.
analysis.power: Large samples; intervals are wide for Native American respondents (AUD 12.1, 9.3-15.6 vs 16.6, 12.7-21.5) and for small subgroups of people who drank at high risk (age 65 or older: 19.8, 13.7-27.8 vs 31.3, 24.8-38.7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Between the 2001-2002 and 2012-2013 surveys, weighted past-year drinking rose from 65.4% to 72.7%, weekly high-risk drinking from 9.7% to 12.6% and past-year DSM-IV AUD from 8.5% to 12.7%, with significant differences in almost every subgroup. In absolute terms the AUD difference was largest at ages 18-29 (+7.2 points), among black respondents (+6.4) and in the lowest income group (+5.8), similar in men (+4.3) and women (+4.1), and smallest at 65 or older (+1.6), whose relative increase (106.7%) is the largest only because their starting prevalence was 1.5% (editors' calculations from Tables 1 to 3).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract, Key Points and Conclusions call the increases a "public health crisis" that portends rises in chronic disease, especially among women, older adults, racial or ethnic minorities and socioeconomically disadvantaged people; the study measured no health outcome, and the Discussion's supporting trends (cardiovascular and stroke mortality, hypertension, cirrhosis deaths, emergency visits) are cited aggregate series. (2) Increases are said to be greatest among women, older adults, minorities and people with less education and income; this holds for relative change only, and no difference in change between subgroups was tested. In absolute terms women's rise in AUD matched men's, and older adults had the smallest rise in both high-risk drinking and AUD. (3) The validity of the increase is defended by coherence with other indicators, but the cited increases are much smaller than NESARC's, the stable NSDUH AUD trend the same group reported in 2015 is not mentioned, and design differences other than response rate are not discussed. (4) The Discussion's explanations of subgroup trends (more permissive norms and career stress for women, wealth inequality after the 2008 recession) were not measured. (5) The Conclusions' statements on low treatment rates (below 10%) and on costs ($250 billion) do not come from this study's data. (6) The Key Points list the relative changes (11.2%, 29.9%, 49.4%) in a way that can be read as prevalences.

timeline.event: Earlier national surveys cited in the Introduction and Discussion: between 1991-1992 and 2001-2002 past-year drinking rose from 44.0% to 65.4%, high-risk drinking from about 8.0% to 9.7% and DSM-IV AUD from 7.4% to 8.5%.
Hasin et al. (2007): NESARC 2001-2002 12-month DSM-IV AUD 8.5%, the baseline here (alcohol evidence map, Tier C).

Grant et al. (2015), NESARC-III DSM-5 AUD 13.9% past year; its Discussion reports that NSDUH 12-month AUD was stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013, against NESARC-III's DSM-IV 12.7% (card sc_grant_2015).
This study: DSM-IV AUD 8.5% to 12.7%, high-risk drinking 9.7% to 12.6%, past-year drinking 65.4% to 72.7%.

Schuckit, accompanying editorial in JAMA Psychiatry (doi 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2017.1981), whose freely visible opening paragraph accepts the paper's case that the US faces a crisis with alcohol use; the rest was not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The NESARC-to-NESARC-III comparison is the main source for a large rise in US past-year AUD between 2001-2002 and 2012-2013. The NSDUH showed no such rise in AUD over the same years (as the same authors reported in 2015), so the size of the change depends on which survey is believed, and this paper cannot separate change in the population from change in the survey. Claims should present the figures as differences between two surveys, give absolute alongside relative change, and say that another national survey did not show the AUD increase. No correction is linked on the PMC or JAMA Psychiatry pages (checked 27 October 2026).

funding.funder: Sponsored by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, with supplemental funding from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, and by National Institutes of Health grant K05AA014223 (Dr Hasin). The funding sources are stated to have had no role in design, conduct, data collection, management, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation, review or approval, or the decision to submit (Article notes › Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor).
funding.affiliations_note: Nine of the 11 authors are at the NIAAA Epidemiology and Biometry Branch, the institute that conducted both surveys; two are at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University. As in the 2015 paper, the no-role statement refers to a sponsor whose staff designed, ran and analysed the surveys. No industry funding or ties are declared. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A bridging design in which the 2001-2002 and 2012-2013 protocols (or the NESARC-III and NSDUH protocols) are fielded on random halves of one sample in the same year would measure how much of the difference in AUD prevalence comes from survey design; a continuing series with an unchanged design would then establish the trend.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Both surveys sample the US household and group-quarters population; homeless and incarcerated people are excluded from both, and the two frames differ in sampling stages and oversampled groups.
Both are multistage probability samples with weights for unequal selection, analysed with design-based standard errors (SUDAAN).
43,093 and 36,309 respondents; small subgroups (Native American respondents; older adults who drank at high risk) have wide intervals.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Field periods, sampling and weighting are described, but the composition of each sample is not tabulated in this paper.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Both surveys are weighted for non-response; the change in response (81.0% to about 60%) between the two surveys is not examined beyond weighting.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Structured DSM-IV interview with reliability cited from the group's own work; self-report only; validity figures for NESARC-III are not given here.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Identical drinking questions and near-identical AUD items, but different instrument versions (AUDADIS-IV and AUDADIS-5) fielded under different protocols 11 years apart; only the effect of the added abuse questions was checked.

Design-based standard errors and t tests are appropriate, but change is reported only in relative terms, subgroup differences in change are asserted without tests, 145 comparisons are made without correction, and one printed interval is implausible.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: 81.0% (NESARC) and about 60% (NESARC-III), managed by weighting; differential response is a direct threat to a comparison between the surveys.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This rating concerns the paper's result, the change between surveys: each survey's own prevalence would rate as moderate (as for sc_grant_2015). The comparison is of two independent surveys whose designs differ in response rate (81.0% vs about 60%), sampling stages, approving bodies and fieldwork, census weighting base and instrument version (a $90 incentive is reported for NESARC-III only); the only comparability check reported concerns three added abuse questions, and another national survey (NSDUH) did not show the AUD rise. The direction of change in drinking is consistent with other indicators, but its size, and the subgroup pattern presented in relative terms, cannot be attributed to the population rather than to the surveys.

key_findings.finding: Samples: NESARC, April 2001 to June 2002, 43,093 adults, overall response 81.0% (sampling frame 98.5%, household 88.5%, person 93.0%), weighted to the 2000 Census; NESARC-III, April 2012 to June 2013, 36,309 adults, household response 72.0%, person 84.0%, overall 60.0%, weighted to the 2012 American Community Survey, with a $90 incentive.
key_findings.note: The Limitations give the NESARC-III response rate as 60.1%; the product of the printed components is 60.5% (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Definitions: a standard drink is 14 g of pure alcohol; high-risk drinking is 4 or more drinks on any day for women or 5 or more for men, exceeded at least weekly in the past 12 months; DSM-IV AUD is 12-month abuse (1 or more of 4 criteria) or dependence (3 or more of 7).

Comparability: past-year alcohol use was asked with identical questions in both surveys; DSM-IV AUD items were virtually identical, with 3 reworded and 3 abuse questions added in NESARC-III. DSM-IV AUD with and without the added questions: 8.5% vs 8.2% in NESARC (kappa 0.97) and 12.7% vs 12.2% in NESARC-III (kappa 0.98).

Past-year alcohol use rose from 65.4% (64.3-66.6) to 72.7% (71.4-73.9), a relative increase of 11.2%, and rose significantly in every subgroup: women 59.6% to 69.0% (+15.8%), men 71.8% to 76.7% (+6.8%), ages 65 or older 45.1% to 55.2% (+22.4%), Asian or Pacific Islander 48.4% to 62.5% (+29.1%), black 53.2% to 66.1% (+24.2%), Hispanic 59.9% to 70.2% (+17.2%), family income below $20,000 52.4% to 64.1% (+22.3%).

Weekly high-risk drinking rose from 9.7% (9.3-10.2) to 12.6% (12.0-13.2), relative +29.9%, significantly in all subgroups except Native American respondents (12.4% to 17.4%) and rural residents (9.6% to 10.8%): women 5.7% to 9.0% (+57.9%), men 14.2% to 16.4% (+15.5%), ages 65 or older 2.3% to 3.8% (+65.2%), black 9.3% to 15.1% (+62.4%), Hispanic 9.6% to 13.5% (+40.6%).

Past-year DSM-IV AUD rose from 8.5% (8.0-8.9) to 12.7% (12.1-13.3), relative +49.4%, significantly in all subgroups except Native American respondents (12.1% to 16.6%) and rural residents (8.8% to 10.2%): women 4.9% to 9.0% (+83.7%), men 12.4% to 16.7% (+34.7%), ages 18-29 16.2% to 23.4% (+44.4%), 65 or older 1.5% to 3.1% (+106.7%), black 6.9% to 13.3% (+92.8%), Hispanic 7.9% to 12.0% (+51.9%), white 8.9% to 13.1% (+47.2%), family income below $20,000 8.8% to 14.6% (+65.9%), urban 8.4% to 13.4% (+59.5%).

Conditional prevalence: DSM-IV AUD among people who drank in the past year rose from 12.9% to 17.5% (+35.7%; not significant for Native American, previously married and rural respondents); among people who drank at high risk, from 46.5% (44.3-48.7) to 54.5% (52.7-56.4) (+17.2%; not significant for Native American, Asian or Pacific Islander, previously married, less-than-high-school, rural, Northeast and Midwest respondents).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th and 5th subsections, 1st paragraph each; Tables 4 and 5
key_findings.note: The 2001-2002 interval for AUD among people who drank is printed as 12.3-17.5 in both the abstract and Table 4 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Absolute changes in percentage points (editors' calculation from Tables 1 to 3): alcohol use +7.3; high-risk drinking +2.9 (women +3.3, men +2.2, ages 65 or older +1.5, 30-44 +4.0); DSM-IV AUD +4.2 (men +4.3, women +4.1, ages 18-29 +7.2, 65 or older +1.6, black +6.4, white +4.2, Hispanic +4.1, Asian or Pacific Islander +3.5, income below $20,000 +5.8, $70,000 or more +3.7).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation; the paper reports relative changes only.

key_findings.finding: The authors translate the prevalences into about 20.2 million (2001-2002) and 29.6 million (2012-2013) adults with high-risk drinking and 17.6 million and 29.9 million with DSM-IV AUD, and contrast the 49.4% rise in AUD with the 14.8% rise between 1991-1992 (7.4%) and 2001-2002 (8.5%).

Corroboration cited by the authors: past-year alcohol use rose 6.0% in the National Health Interview Survey and 9.1% in the NSDUH over the same period, drinking 5 or more drinks at least once in the past year rose 17.8% in the NHIS, and per capita consumption from sales rose 6.4%. No other survey's AUD trend is cited.

Limitations stated by the authors: no biological testing; homeless and incarcerated people not covered (possible underestimation); lay interviewers, though a NESARC-III substudy is said to show good concordance with clinician diagnoses; NESARC-III response (60.1%) lower than NESARC's (81.0%), with weighting said to facilitate comparison; validity of the increases supported, in their view, by coherence with other indicators.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2001-2002 prevalence of DSM-IV AUD among people who drank in the past year is printed as 12.9% with a 95% CI of 12.3%-17.5%, in both the abstract and Table 4; the upper limit equals the 2012-2013 point estimate and makes the interval about eight times wider above the estimate than below it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Almost certainly a transcription error (the same error appears on the JAMA Psychiatry page); the upper limit should not be quoted. By the widths of the neighbouring intervals the true upper limit is probably near 13.5%, but that is an inference.

reporting_issues.issue: The NESARC-III overall response rate is 60.0% in the Methods and 60.1% in the Limitations; the product of the printed household (72.0%) and person (84.0%) rates is 60.5% (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote about 60% with the components.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the high school (10.4% to 14.8%) and some college or higher (9.5% to 11.6%) rows lack the significance marker, although the text says high-risk drinking rose significantly in all subgroups except Native American and rural respondents and the two years' intervals do not overlap.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting omission; both increases are significant by the paper's own test.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion refers to changes between the early 1900s and the early 2000s where the early 1990s are meant, and gives the earlier rise in DSM-IV AUD (7.4% to 8.5%) as 14.8% and, two sentences later, as 14.9% (14.9% by editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the three additional abuse questions appeared in NESARC-III, yet report a comparison of DSM-IV AUD with and without the additional questions for NESARC as well (8.5% vs 8.2%, kappa 0.97), without saying how the comparison was made in a survey that did not ask them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparability check for the 2001-2002 survey cannot be understood from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Points state that alcohol use (11.2%), high-risk drinking (29.9%) and DSM-IV AUD (49.4%) increased, giving relative changes without labelling them as such.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take 49.4% for a prevalence or an absolute change; the absolute change in AUD was 4.2 percentage points.
